title: Nokia CEO says data centers would be built '2x faster' without supply constraints
source_used: Briefs Finance, Digital Today and TokenPost, all relaying CNBC's interview; the CNBC page (pool link) returned HTTP 403
key_facts: Nokia president and chief executive Justin Hotard spoke on CNBC's The Tech Download podcast; CNBC published the interview on 5 Oct 2026.
He pushed back on the idea that data centers are being overbuilt, saying that if the industry could build twice as fast, customers probably would.
Shortages of key memory chips and constraints on energy are the two chokepoints the relays name as slowing construction.
Hotard said that even if no new frontier AI model came out in the next three years, the industry could make tremendous progress just deploying today's technology.
He did not quantify the shortages or how much faster construction could move in practice (TokenPost).
Nokia, headquartered in Espoo, Finland, supplies hardware that links chips inside data centers and ties facilities together; its shares are up about 130% over the past year.
A projection cited by the relays puts US investment in AI-related buildings, power, networks and chips at $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032; it is a projection, not completed spending.
quote_evidence: Nokia CEO Justin Hotard told CNBC that if bottlenecks eased, customers would likely build data centers at double today's pace.
Two practical chokepoints keep coming up: limited supplies of key memory chips and constraints on energy.
He did not quantify the shortages or how much faster construction could move in practice.
why_it_matters_hint: A supplier's chief executive says chips and power, not demand, are what hold back the AI data center buildout.
notes: CNBC is the first reporter. Its page returned 403, so the entry relies on Briefs Finance, Digital Today and TokenPost, which agree on the quotes. The remark is a company chief's opinion, and Nokia sells equipment for the buildout.
